Before the Orders of the Day are called, I wish to ask the Prime Minister a question. On the 22nd of February the matter to which I wish to refer was under discussion, and after it had been pointed out that there was no provision in the Railway Act, the right hon. gentleman said :
I must say that I have a confession to make to the House, and a confession that is not pleasant to me. I did not know '.hat the commission was not only not empowered hut not obliged to make a report. I have always understood that it was part of the duty of the commission to make a yearly report of their operations ; not only of the money which we gave them to spend as to how they have expended it-and for this we are responsible to parliament-but also of their operations, what they have done, what cases they have decided, so that the public could know exactly what has taken place. We have a right to that information, and if it is found after a conference with the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways, who is more familiar than I am with the Act, that the commission is not bound to make such a report,
I think we should enact legislation this very session to have such a report from the commission. I shall at once call the attention of the Minister of Justice to this. If the commission is not under obligation to make such a report it is due to parliament that it should be at once put under such an obligation.
I wisb to ask the right bou. gentleman if that conference with the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Railways has taken place and with what result ? I ask this question as I do not see that any legislation has been introduced.
Sir WILFRID LAUR'IER. I understand that a report will be ready in a very short time.

I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to a matter which came up on Wednesday. In reply to a question from me regarding the report of the Railway Commission, that lion, minister said :
I would say to my hon. friend that the report has not been laid before the House and the department is not in a position to lay such a report on the table, but as soon as I am in a position to do so I will submit It to the House.
Further on, when I called attention to the fact that a promise had been made, and that it was difficult to understand why the hon. minister did not carry out his promise, he said :
I think my hon. friend must be under some misapprehension as to any assurance that I gave him in respect to the placing of such a report upon the table of the House. I said that I would exercise due diligence in endeavouring to get that report and that I had been assured by the railway commissioners that such a report would be prepared. I have not received such a complete report. I was mixing up the two commissions. You are asking in respect to the Railway Commission ?
The Board of Railway Commissioners.

I have not received that complete report yet, but I am expecting it.
As the hon. minister seemed to be under the impression that no definite promise had been made, il took occasion on Wednesday, to show that such a promise had been made at least two months previous. On the 3rd March the hon. minister then said :
I had a conference with the chairman of the Railway Commission, and he stated that the secretary of the commission was now preparing such a report. As soon as it is placed in my hands I will lay it on the table of the House.
Can the hon. minister state any definite time when it will be ready ?

I did not ask the exact date. Only to-day the chairman assured me that It was being prepared, but I did not ask whether it would be ready in a day or two. I assumed it would be ready in the near future.
Again speaking definitely on the 17th March, exactly two months ago, he said :
A report has been promised, and I hope to have it within a few days.
Not only on the two occasions I have referred to, but also on the 22nd February we were definitely given to understand that a report would be brought down without delay. In view of all these promises, it was rather extraordinary that two days ago the minister said he never did make any definite promise and was not in a position to make one. In fact the matter seemed to have slipped from his mind altogether. Not only is that the unfortunate position of things, but we have not yet had the amendment to the statute which the First Minister promised us on the 22nd February nor can we get any definite information about it. It is very unfortunate that this omission should have occurred in the Railway Act, but apart altogether from that Act, we would have expected the Railway Commission to have had a specific report ready before parliament met. Not only should we have from this Railway Commission a general report on that branch of the service which is costing the people so much money, but we should have a special

report from the late chairman of the commission (Mr. Blair) who made a special toui-in the United States in order to acquire some expert knowledge of the working of commissions of this kind. The report of the Railway Commission itself as to all its doings and all its expenditure should have been in the hands of the Minister of Railways before parliament assembled and that report should have been embodied in the report of the minister. Yet we have the unfortunate condition of things that the minister was bound to admit two days ago that he knows practically nothing about the matter yet, that he has taken no definite action to procure definite information which the House required and as far as he is concerned it had practically slipped from his mind. Now having called the attention of the minister to it in this way I trust that some effort will be made to have this report laid upon the table of the House at once so that we may know what this commission is doing, particularly as it is a new departure, and we should be able to judge whether it is carrying out the expectations which those who framed the Act had in view at the time the Railway Act, 1903, was introduced.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMERSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext: On Wednesday I stated that I codld not give any definite assurance as to the time when the report from the Railway Commission could be expected. I had at that time in mind the fact that I had on a former occasion expressed to the House my hope that I would soon be in a position to lay on the table of the House the report of that board for the reason that I had been told by the chairman that such a report was in course of preparation. I have not yet received that report although I have looked for it on more than one occasion. I have however some assurance and hope that I will be able to place it on the table by Monday next at the latest. I of course am dependent upon the Railway Commissioners in the matter. It is not something under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals ; I cannot force the commission to make a report, as it does not emanate from my department, and therefore I cannot be held responsible for its non-production, but I shall hope that it may be forthcoming at least by Monday next.

On March 3rd this question was first asked, something over two and a half months ago, and now the minister admits that he cannot force the commissioners to submit a report to him. That is one very good, strong reason why an amendment to the Railway Act should have been introduced compelling the Railway Commission to make a report to this House. The people of this country are expending large sums of money for the purpose of having a Railway Commission, and that parliament is to be deprived of all control over that Itail-Mr. LENNOX.
way Commission is something I cannot understand, and I think in view of the statement made by the First Minister the government are a little lax in introducing their amendment to the Railway Bill. In this particular instance, I think parliament is entitled to a report and that steps should be taken at the earliest possible moment to have the Act amended in that direction.

I would like to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to his words on February 22. He says now that he has no control over these gentlemen, but on page 1532 of the Revised ' Hansard ' he says:
I am only endeavouring to point out wliat I consider to be the law. I am quite free to admit that there should be a report from the commission. I am quite in accord with what has been stated in that regard, and I think that the commissioners should make a report from time to time to the Governor in Council through the Department of Railways and Canals, for as my hon. friend from Simooe (Mr. Lennox) says, if this commission is not in any way connected with the government through the Department of Railways and Canals, he cannot see any other department by which it would be thus connected. I quite agree with him that the natural avenue and channel between that board and the government is through the Department of Railways and Canals, but it does not seem to me that the Act makes proper provision for that.
The minister on that occasion admitted that there should be a provision for a report and that immediate steps should be taken to force the commission If they would not act, and that such a provision should be introduced at once if it was not already in the Railway Act. We have had no intimation that any step has been taken towards a remedy of that very peculiar omission which occurs in the Railway Act.

I quite adhere to my expressions of a former date in connection with a report from that commission. I might state to my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) that he need not become suddenly impatient. There seems to be some weeks, at least some days before us, before the close of this session, and we must remember that there are quite a number of amendments under consideration ; a Bill is now on the order paper making amendments to the Railway Act, and before that Bill goes through and is considered by the committee I think that it will be my duty and privilege to submit to the House some amendments and among these there may be found one that will cure the defect in the Act in connection with the report. We have been pretty well occupied during this session with work ; at least there have been Bills that have received a little consideration, and I would not wish to interfere in any way with the progress of matters of that kind with any legislation affecting railways, but the Railway Department will have its turn in connection with legislation

and I hope my hon. friend will not be too impatieHt.

I do not think it is quite fair for the hon. Minister of Railways to suggest that the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is impatient in this matter. We have been here four or five months waiting for legislation from the government and have had only one piece of legislation which my hon. friend properly says has taken up a good deal of time. But that is not the fault of the opposition but the fault of the legislation which the government has introduced. It is legislation which is very controversial and very peculiar. This Railway Commission was appointed two years ago and for two years the Dominion of Canada has had that commission, but the people have had not a tittle of official evidence or information as to what that commission is doing, not one particle of information have the people of Canada as to whether that commission is doing anything like what was expected when it was appointed. I have a good deal of respect for the commission as a whole and for the individual members of it, but this is an instance where all public servants will do as they like if there is not some restraining or guiding hand in the shape of legislation or rules to govern them to which they must submit. Instead of lecturing the House and the hon. member who spoke in the interests of the people, I think the Minister of Railways or some member of the government should apologize to the House and the country for their laxity in this matter. It is not a matter that should be treated with levity. We have a large expenditure connected with this Railway Commission, and they were appointed to do work that is most important to the country. We do not know nor do the people of the country know at all except in cases where they have hunted up information for themselves,-sometimes at a good deal of expense, and always with a good deal of trouble,-what that commission is doing. They are not responsible apparently to the Minister of Railways or to the government in the matter of making a report. I do not see why there was not legislation introduced last session in this connection for this matter was known last session. On February 22 of this year as has been said, attention was drawn to it and the hon. member for South Simcoe then brought the matter up. The Prime Minister on that occasion said :
I shall at once call the attention of the Minister of Justice to this. If the commission is not under obligation to make such a report it is due to parliament that it should be at once put under such an obligation.
That was on the 22nd of February of this year, and here we are practically three months later and nothing has been done. Now ' at once ' might mean, I should think less than three months' time. Parliament
is in session and I do think we ought to have a little more speed in this matter. To-day we were promised in a very cursory, almost off-handed way by the minister. that there will be some other measure in regard to the amendment of the Railway Act which is supposed to be dealt with this session and which is now on the order paper. It is certainly as important as any legislation that has been introduced by the government, or promised by the government. I do not think that the manner in which the Minister of Railways treats this House would inspire the public with much hope that the government are going to do any better in the future than they have been doing the last few years ; and if not, I think the censure of the people should be visited upon this government. I would urge upon the government, so far as I have any influence, at least I would request the government as representing my constituency in this House, to take immediate action. I do not wish to allow this occasion to go by without putting on record my protest and the protest of my constituents against the dilatoriness with which the government has treated this matter, the want of care, the lack of appreciation of the importance of the matter, which I think the government has evinced. This' matter is one which demands a remedy at once, and we ought to have better assurance than we have yet had from the Minister of Railways that it will be attended to, and that the Railway Commission will be charged with the duty of making this report, either quarterly, half yearly or yearly, at all events at some set time, when these reports will become public documents and open to inspection by the public, so that the people can learn what is going on with regard to this matter, and all those other numerous matters that the commission has to deal with. The House desires to learn how the commission is working, and whether any other amendments are required in order to make it fulfil the intention of its appointment.

I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Railways to a condition of affairs that I think requires his attention and the attention of the commission. I refer to rates that are charged by American roads entering Canada and passing through this country What we ask is that the same rates, the same conditions and the same privileges be demanded of them as they are obliged to grant to the people of the United States. I think this proposition is reasonable and fair, and I know it is one of great moment to the people of Ontario. The American roads entering Canada name what rates they like on commodities originating in the states for people in Canada, but when they enter Canadian territory they do not give proportionate rates. We ask that this matter be taken into consideration, and if the facts

justify it, that the matter be laid before the commission to be dealt with 'by them. Let me say a word with reference to the commission and its acts during the past year. If there is any one who is not familiar with the decisions that have been rendered by that commission I think he has himself to blame. I do not think there is a farmer in Canada to-day but knows of the sweeping decisions that have been made with regard to rates on cattle and rates on graiD. The decisions given in favour of manufacturers in regard to rates, so far as those decisions are obligatory, have been of such importance that to-day the commission is swamped with appeals ; no less than 1,450 complaints have been placed before the commission since it was appointed, and tne great bulk of them I think have been disposed of. The position of American roads running through Canada has been so well discussed that it is not necessary for me to refer to it at any length now. I hope, however, that the tariffs, the minimums, and also the classifications affecting shippers, will be looked into, and that they will be made applicable to conditions existing in this country, and we firmly believe that a solution will be found to the present difficulties aud complaints that require to be remedied.

speechtext:

Has the hon. Postmaster General (Sir William Mulock) any account of that ?
I do not know anything about the item. I have no doubt that $1,000 is a small item in the department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would like to inquire
if any portion of this sum is required to pay the salary of this postmaster ? Just for the information of the hon. Postmaster General I will read a portion of a letter that has been sent to me. It is as follows :
Now, Mr. Taylor, I beg your kind indulgence . for a few moments while I call your attention to the way in which the deputy returning officer and his poll clerk conducted the election proceedings at polling division No. 3, Kitley, where I was agent in your behalf. The deputy returning officer was George Milton Leverette, the village postmaster, and his polling clerk was Benjamin Franklin Stewart, a carriage maker. From the opening to the closing of the poll the deputy returning officer ran things with a high hand. Everything was trampled under foot. Oaths of office, the statutes and myself, not physically but officially, were trampled under foot and completely ignored. Never did I see such brazen defiance of law and right. It was plainly manifest that 'he Grit machine was doing business at the old stand as brisk as ever and had established a local branch at Frank-ville under management of the deputy returning officer and his poll clerk. To enumerate some of the violations of the law committed by these two election officials, I wish to say that the deputy returning officer in defiance of a protest from me placed the ballot box on the floor to the right of his chair ; when so placed it was behind the table and entirely out of the view of those present. I read the law to him, but he emphatically told me it was on the floor and was going to stay there and I might help myself if I could. All that was left for me to do was to seat myself on a chair beside it, which I did. Another thing, he said he did not have the required statutory dates to be inserted in the oath to voters, but I really did not believe him. Fortunately, however, I supplied this want by having them myself under certificate of the township clerk, otherwise I do not believe I should have been able to have sworn a voter at all that day. Again, he allowed his poll clerk to act as agent for your opponent, Gibson, in the absence of duly appointed agents.
I protested, but was powerless. The poll clerk told a voter, one Frank Livingston, whom I

challenged, that I .vas doing dirty work, and was only tryiag to bluff him out of his good vote. Through these encouraging words of the poll clerk the voter took the oath and voted. To-day he stands a perjured man. Something more yet. The deputy returning officer put some private mark or number on the stub of the ballots besides the number he was entitled by law to put on the counterfoil. Here again,
I protested, but was told that he was doing so and would continue to do so and 1 might help myself if I could. I asked to see that private mark or number, but was refused. Now, Mr. Taylor, if I could afford the expense I would go to Gananoque to see you personally about these matters. -Something should be done. An example should be made of these two election officials because if not they will be bolder than ever the next time. The matter, however, will be left entirely in your hands. Many Conservatives here say that the matter should be attended to and that prosecutions should follow. As for the deputy returning officer, you can do what you like with him. You can bring his case up on the floor of the House next session or deal with him otherwise as you think best.
I would like to inquire of the hon. Postmaster General if any portion of this sum is to pay that man's salary. I draw these facts to the hon. minister's attention. There is his officer, a postmaster, drawing probably $1,000 a year salary, and yet he goes and acts as a partisan, ignores the law and conducts an election in the manner here described.

No portion of this item will go to pay the salary of any postmaster. There is in the estimates always an item for salaries. If my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) will turn to the estimates he will find that that is so. Having made an explanation and as this matter is not connected with this item I have nothing further to say, but if it is proposed to continue the discussion perhaps there may be some further question that would occur to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I want to know if the hon. gentleman approves of this conduct on the part of one of his postmasters, and if any portion of this amount is to pay his salary will he spend some of it in conducting an investigation into the actions of one of his officers who has conducted himself in this way ? I should further like to ask the hon. gentleman, if the investigation shows that these statements are correct, will he dismiss his official ?

I should think this is not the tribunal to deal with the conduct of men who are engaged in conducting an election. There is a way of reaching them under the election law. If I correctly heard my hon. friend reading that letter it was written prior to the meeting of the House and he has had it for many months in his possession. The law gives him a remedy. Every person who undertakes to act as an officer of the Crown in conducting an election is bound to conform to the law,
and if he fails to conform to the law the law is within the reach of every person, my hon. friend and all others, and there are officers whose duty it is to prosecute persons who violate the Election Act It is not the duty of the Postmaster General. It is the duty of the officers who are engaged in the administration of criminal justice to prosecute. I know nothing about the matter. I do not even know the name of the person, and it would be an extraordinary thing if I had to inquire into the conduct of officers as to the manner in which they might or might not have conducted themselves when they were appointed to positions having nothing whatever to do with their positions connected with this department.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite right in saying that this letter was written some time ago, but this is the first opportunity I have had of dealing with the matter. When the estimates of the Post Office Department were taken up I embraced the first opportunity I had.
We passed sup-plementaries months ago.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I was not present when the items of the Post Office Department came up or I certainly should have referred to this matter then. Will the hon. Postmaster General allow one of his paid servants, drawing a salary of probably $1,000 a year, to accept a position as deputy returning officer at an election and violate the Election Act in a partisan manner as this postmaster has done ? I gave the hon. Postmaster General his name. It is Mr. Leverette, postmaster at Frankville. If public officials are at liberty to run post offices and to act as partisan agents the country ought to know it. The country authorizes him to employ these officials but he says he is not responsible for their conduct. He says that the hon. member can take proceedings under the law. There are the courts of law, but I want to take the proper course. I bring it to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General, and I ask him to deal with it, or let the country know that postmasters and all other officials under this government are at liberty to do as they please, that while being paid for their services by the country they may at the same time conduct themselves as offensive partisans.

I think it is no part of my duty as Postmaster General to inquire into the manner in which officials of my department may have conducted themselves, should they be appointed to such positions as those of deputy returning officers. I have not heard of this man's existence until this minute, and I do believe it has been the practice throughout Canada under all governments from time to time to make use of various officials for the proper conduct of

elections. If these officials in the discharge of their duties as election clerks, or poll clerks, or returning officers do not comply with the election laws they are amenable to these laws. It is not my duty to follow them in all their other spheres of life ; my duty is confined to seeing that they perform their duties as postmasters, and if they undertake other duties they become answerable to some other tribunal, and that is the tribunal to which my hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) should appeal. This is not the place to try that question, and I think my hon. friend would be more in order by referring the conduct of this gentleman as returning officer, to his superior in that capacity who would be interested in maintaining the proper management of elections.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Postmaster General knows that he has dismissed a great many postmasters throughout Canada for alleged political interference, and only yesterday we had the case of a postmaster with a salary of $25 who was dismissed simply because he exercised the right of franchise. Here is a man with a salary of probably $1,000, and he can be as offensive a partisan as he likes, and when I ask the Postmaster General to investigate and have him dismissed if the charge is correct, the Postmaster General says he will not interfere;
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) asked me if I would investigate the manner in which this gentleman acted as returning officer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Certainly, I asked the Postmaster General to investigate the charge that this postmaster has been an offensive partisan in not discharging his duty faithfully and in doing it in an offensive partisan manner. If that is true the postmaster should be dismissed.

The hon. gentleman is evidently mixing up his grievances, and he does not make clear what he really desifes. I understand from his letter and from his remarks that this officer is charged with two offences, but I thought the gravamen of the hon. gentleman's charge was that this postmaster had not properly conducted an election, and not that he was an offensive partisan in the discharge of his post office duties. The hon. gentleman referred to this man having placed a ballot box in some place contrary to law, and he seemed to dwell upon that feature of the charge. My remarks were directed to that, and I say that as to the manner in which he may have acted as an officer for the proper conduct of elections it is not for me to interfere. If there is a charge that he has contravened any of the rules of conduct for a postmaster it is my duty to investigate.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: That is all I ask.

If the hon. gentleman will send me a charge against this postmaster in that respect I will have it investigated, but I would not feel at liberty to inquire into his alleged misconduct as a returning officer.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have made my charge here and the Postmaster General will see it written down verbatim in ' Hansard ' to-morrow, and every word that appears in ' Hansard ' will be substantiated. This man has acted illegally, and I ask if it is the policy of the government to let their postmasters act as deputy returning officers in an offensive partisan manner ?
Let us not misunderstand. My hon. friend mixes up his grievances.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I mixed up nothing ; I read the letter.

He asks whether or not it is the policy of the government to allow postmasters to act as deputy returning officers in an offensive manner. It is not the policy of the department to allow postmasters to assist in an offensive manner under any circumstances, either as deputy returning officers or in any other capacity, and I am quite willing to investigate that branch of my hon. friend's complaint. If there is a complaint that as a deputy returning officer this man contravened the election law, I do not think my hon. friend will expect me to inquire into that phase of his conduct. I am quite prepared to take my hon. friend's speech and the letter, in the light that I interpret it and so far as this man's conduct as postmaster is concerned I am quite prepared to investigate that.

Will the Postmaster General tell us what he thinks about allowing postmasters to act as deputy returning officers at all ? The Postmaster General says that this. House is not a tribunal for trying election cases, but I would remind him that it is a tribunal for trying the conduct of the Post Office Department. Does the Postmaster General want us to understand that he has no objection whatever of opportunity for money being embezzled cers ? I will leave out of the question for the moment whether this postmaster acted in an offensive way or not; I will not consider whether it may be another case of opportunity for money being embezzled) while the postmaster is not in charge of his office ; but I would ask the Postmaster Gem eral if he thinks that a postmaster should act as a deputy returning officer when in the discharge of his duties as such he must of necessity be away from his post office from about half-past eight in the morning until six o'clock on the evening of election day ? Does the Postmaster General think that is right ? The Postmaster relies upon the technicality, that he cannot investigate

this man's conduct as deputy returning officer but that he can investigate it as postmaster, and that being so does he believe that the postmaster should tor an entire day be absent from the post office. We all know that the party in power selects these deputy returning officers from amongst men of their own political persuasion, but I will not press that particular phase of the question for the moment. I wish to know now from the Postmaster General if he approves of postmasters acting in a capacity which must keep them away from their post offices for an entire day ?

I am prepared to state here that the postmaster in question, Mr. Leverette, is a first-class man, and I say further that he is a man who would transact any business he has to do in a proper way. If he is a returning officer he is a man who will discharge his duties in a legal manner, and as postmaster or in any other capacity he will be found to be a faithful officer. But, to expect that a man who only gets a couple of hundred dollars per year for running a post office shall devote all his time to that office is perfect nonsense. Such a man must undertake any business that comes in his way. I have no doubt that Mr. Leverette when he does vote will vote Liberal, and vote against the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor), but I am satisfied that he will be found to be honest and faithful in the discharge of any duties that are entrusted to him.

I can tell my hon. friends opposite that I have a case in my county of a somewhat similar kind to that which we are now discussing. In the town in which I live the postmaster is Mr. J. B. Pearce, a Conservative who has been twenty years in the post office, and I can prove that he went out and canvassed against me, and canvassed strongly against me too.

The Postmaster General since he came to office has established some very bad precedents which he now finds are embarrassing. The rule used to be that every postmaster except those in cities and towns had a right to be an active partisan in an election if he wished. Because he held a little post office worth $7 or $8 a year, he was not to be debarred from taking part on behalf of either the Conservative or the Reform candidate ; and I think that was the true principle. That, principle has been infringed upon by the Postmaster General, who has dismissed this postmaster without a trial and after he denied being an active partisan. It was sufficient for the hon. Postmaster General to get a note from the member of the House saying that a certain postmaster had been an active partisan in the election, and he was dismissed. I have heard the Postmaster General asked in this House if there
had been an investigation, and his reply was :	No, it was a sufficient reason for
him to receive information from the member representing the riding that a postmaster had been an active partisan. It is small politics for any representative of the government to interfere with that kind of officer. Except in cities and towns, postmasters have a right to be active partisans on either side if they wish, and there should be no interference with them by the Postmaster General or any other person as to
how they voted.

I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart), and I will tell you how this matter has been managed in the county of Norfolk up to the present time. The local member, Mr. W. A. Charlton, the late Speaker of the Ontario legislature, was the postmaster for many years at a small village called Lyndoch. He did not attend to the post office himself, but one of his clerks did so. Mr. Charlton always stumped the riding against me. I was applied to in regard to this, but I declined to interfere with him for any political act. I said that if any one had a charge to make as to the way the office was run, I would see that it would be investigated and dealt with. In two of my elections, another gentleman who was a postmaster, and is still postmaster, though his father ran the post office while he lived two miles from the village, was president of the Reform Association and an active opponent of mine. The same kind of application was made to me with regard to him ; but I declined to go further than to have an Investigation made into any charge that might be made against him in connection with the work of the post office. We have never introduced this small politics into the county on either side. So far this has been the rule followed by this government. I agree with the hon. member for South Lanark that outside of cities and towns, where postmasters are paid for giving their whole time to the .service, there should be no interference with postmasters. It is a shameful practice on either side in regard to these petty offices, and I would oppose my own party indulging in it, whatever anybody else might think about it. I would be opposed to it even in retaliation. I..L folk we have strenuous politics, but we have never found it necessary to resort to that

But the policy adopted by the Postmaster General, when a Conservative postmaster is complained against, though he does nothing more than vote, is to dismiss him without trial.
There is no such case on record, as a man dismissed because he voted. Every postmaster has a right to vote as he likes, and he has never been interfered with.

I want to give the case of a man who was dismissed simply for voting. The postmaster of Beauharnois, named Doutre, was dismissed because he voted. He never took any other part in the election, and there was no investigation into his case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This concern at New York is making notes for banks the wide world over and is making notes for many countries. Some countries have their own printing departments. In the United States; they have a printing, bureau, but this company with headquarters in New York rnakek notes for banks the world over and for a; number of countries. It is an old estabi lished institution of the highest reputation,! and I have no reason to doubt that all safeguards that we could impose are in force now.

I had reason to inquire into the matter some time ago when I was in charge of the Post Office Department, and I found that in Great Britain and in all countries in Europe it is put under the charge of a certain department and then when the printing is done by c(intract as it is done in England, it is under the supervision of the Inland Revenue Department there and a most accurate supervision as to the paper and everything in reference to it is maintained. There is extreme danger in a company that has a contract with the government having an unlimited right of printing Dominion notes without the supervision of the government. The same thing refers to postage and inland revenue stamps, and I think there should be an efficient government supervision over them even when the work is done by contract.

What difference would it make if a bank were to issue ten ones instead of a ten dollar bill or five ones instead of a five dollar bill ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The main point is that you have to supply the needed currency to meet the demands of the expanding trade and commerce of our country, and if you took the united subscribed capital of all the banks and issued an equal amount of currency you would find a stringency in the money market, because you would not have enough to carry on the business of the country. If the banks want to issue more notes all they have to do is to put up more capital. Whether a note is issued in the denomination of one dollar or five dollars makes no difference in this respect. The subscribed capital of the united banks of the country is not nearly enough to carry on the business of the country.
Is it not a fact that the government of Canada are making a great deal of money in the issuing of these notes in denominations of ones, twos and fours ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I have already stated there is a point-it used to be $25,000,000, but we increased it a year or two ago-up to which we are obliged to carry a reserve of 25 per cent of gold. As respects that there is a profit to the country ; but after you pass that point, for every additional note you issue, you have to put up dollar for dollar and therefore there is no profit in it. We increased the limit in 1903 and that perhaps will meet to some extent the suggestion of my hon. friend from Halton (Mr. Henderson). It used to be $25,000,000, but believing that with the growth and expansion of Canada, we could issue a larger sum on the 25 per cent limit we expanded that in 1903 to $30,000,000, and as the country grows that limit will be raised. There is a certain sum which we may issue with a reserve of 25 per cent of gold. As respects that there is a profit, but when

you pass that point for' every dollar you issue you must have a dollar in gold against it and there is no profit on that.
What is the amount you are allowed to issue on the 25 per cent basis ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
That is $7,000,000 besides the $25,000,000. That makes $32,000,-
000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was increased by the Act of 1903 to $30,000,000.
That $30,000,000 you only have to cover by a reserve of 25 per cent ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That is correct. By the Act, 3 Ed. VIII, Chap. 43, respecting Dominion Notes, it is provided that:
The Minister of Finance and Receiver General shall always hold as security for the redemption of Dominion notes issued and outstanding at any one time, up to and including $30,000,000, an amount in gold, or in gold and securities of Canada, the principal or interest of such securities being guaranteed by the government of the United Kingdom, equal to not less than 25 per cent of the amount of such notes so issued and outstanding.
Does the country make enough money to cover the amount of $140,000 a year that is now being spent for the printing of these notes ? I want to know whether the country Is redeeming this expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think we do until we reach a certain amount. As respects the first sum there is a profit, but for every additional dollar we issue there is no profit.

If we are not making much out of it why should we not allow the different chartered banks to issue these notes ? We look upon our banking system as a very good one and that being so why should not we allow them to issue these notes of the denominations of one, two and four dollars ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of convenience it is better that the banks should issue notes of a certain class and that we should issue notes of a certain class, but it would make no difference if they issued ten ones instead of issuing one ten.

'If their circulation helps them as they say it does, why should we not give them this privilege ? There are some people in Ottawa who are making money only out of circulation. If that Is so, by circulating $39,000,000 or $40,000,000 in ones, twos or threes, it would help them to increase not only their circulation but their capital.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Why not ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Circulation does not help them to increase capital. Capital helps them to increase circulation. They must issue their circulation on the basis of their capital. If a bank has a capital of $1,000,000 and it has only $500,000 or $600,000 of notes out, if the business has only taken up that amount, it has then $400,000 which it can issue in money, and if its own business is not expanding it can loan these notes to another bank, but the moment it l'eaches the limit of its capital it must stop. That is where the government comes in and supplies the difference.
Cannot the Finance Minister find a way to compel the banks to issue clean notes, just as the Dominion is doing ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have not thought it necessary to do more than to generally indicate to the banks that they should pay attention to the cleanliness of the notes in circulation, and I think they are doing so. The Dominion notes in circulation are vastly improved in that respect, and I think the bank notes too. We have not taken any legislative power to compel the banks, but I have no doubt they will pay attention to the matter as a result of the discussion that has taken place here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think it is necessary.
I hear constant complaint of the dirty bills circulated by the banks being injurious to health.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Most of us are so happy to get these bills that we do not quarrel about their shape and colour, but I trust the discussion to-day may induce the banks to give attention to the matter.
The Minister of Finance is of course hot making any personal reference because the members are paid by cheques, the face value of which is very small I am sorry to say.
I assume it would not cost less to print a one dollar note than it would to print a ten dollar note, and if that be the case it would seem that the point is well taken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course it makes no difference in the cost of printing whether the figure be a ' I ' or a ' X ' but it has been found a matter of public convenience that these small notes should be dealt with by the Dominion, and I do not think there is any complaint about it. With the extending business of the country the banks as a rule are able to find employment for their circulation on the basis of the present arrangement.
There is no complaint if we do not lose money in connection with it.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Minister of Finance has told us that there are $47,000,000 now in circulation ; has he ever had a calculation made as to how much of that is lost yearly through fires, &c. Does he think that seven millions of that forty-seven millions have been lost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Once it is issued it is charged up as a part of the debt of this country and must always remain so until it is redeemed. Therefore, whether it is lost or not does not. concern us. True it could never be presented, but it still stands in our books as part of the debt due by the Dominion. We never write off a note until it is redeemed and destroyed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understand that a good share of the profit of the banks is due to the loss of notes in circulation ; there is hardly a fire that there are not some bills lost.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There was a question in olden times as to banks making profit in that way, but I do not think they claim today that they have a right to make such profit. Until a note is redeemed it is held to be a debt of the bank. In olden times there was a practice of writing off notes of that character, but I do not think that practice is followed by the banks to-day.
Although the amount in circulation according to the books of the Finance Department is forty-seven millions, it may not be more than forty millions ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There would not be so much as that lost.

In the many years during which these notes have been in circulation 1 have no doubt that several millions have been lost. I would ask the Finance Minister to tell me, if he thinks it is perfectly safe to issue thirty millions on the basis of 25 per cent of gold, why is it not perfectly safe to issue fifty millions ? Where would be the difficulty ? What reason does the Minister of Finance give for not issuing the entire amount on the basis of 25 per ceut gold ? speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I fear that all the great financial authorities of the world will say that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) is touching on dangerous ground. His proposition simply means what was at one time irreverently called the rag-baby scheme of currency ; grinding out the notes as fast as any one took them up and making money in that way. The financiers of the world have not regarded that system with approval. If Canada adopted the policy of issuing notes on the credit of the country without regard to limit, while we might have great pride in that as Canadians, the financial authorities of the world would not consider that our credit was thereby made good.

It has been suggested that of the forty-seven, million dollars worth of notes in circulation possibly seven mlll-iions may have been destroyed. On the other hand is there not a possibility that several millions of notes now in circulation may be counterfeit ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think not. I appreciate what hon. gentlemen have said as to the necessity of extra precaution, but I think we generally discover counterfeit notes very quickly. There have been a few instances and we have traced them and generally succeeded in finding the counterfeiters in a short time and putting them behind the bars. It is quite a long time since we heard of any Canadian counterfeit notes, and so far as I know there are none to-day. We have taken all reasonable precautions, but in the light of what has been said to-day it will be my duty to look into the matter to see if there is any other precaution which can be taken to prevent the possibility of the occurence of that which my hon. friends fear.
Is it not possible for us to have a definite knowledge of the value of the Dominion notes now in circulation ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We can only give to the public a definite knowledge as to the number issued. What becomes of them is beyond our knowledge and control. We are bound to asume for the purposes of accounts and public credit that they are existing somewhere, and so they stand on the records as a charge against us.

With reference to the thirty million dollars in our treasury, of course I do not want to ask where it is at present, but I wish to know whether n large portion or any portion of that gold is deposited in the banks of this counti*y, and whether we are receiving interest on it *

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No portion of this is held by banks in the way of ordinary deposits ; it is held in other ways. Of course we have our transactions with the banks in other respects and large sums of money are moving to and fro, but these moneys are not included in such bank accounts.

Hear, hear.

Of course I am not personally interested in any way, but sometimes we'hear the statement made, especially during election campaigns, that there is a chest here in which that gold is kept, and very often we hear it said on the platform that the Liberal candidate was up in Ottawa

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is that ?

There is an idea in the country that there is a chest sortie where here in Ottawa where you keep this large amount of gold, and speakers on the stump say : so and so is a thief, because he was seen in Ottawa with his arms as far as his elbows down in the gold. speechtext: House in committee on Bill (No. 152) for the relief of Clara Bidwell McDermot.-Mr. Campbell.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext:
This is a very peculiar case, and I think the Bill ought to stand until the Minister of Justice is present. I have read the evidence, and I am bound to say that I do not think the preamble is proven. I am quite satisfied that no judge of ex-Mr. W. WRIGHT.
perience and no intelligent jury would find this respondent guilty of the allegations which are said by the preamble to be proven on the evidence printed and laid before the House. One does not like to discuss the details of these eases in public more than is necessary ; but we have a public duty to perform. The whole evidence is that of two, women, who notoriously and openly state their reasons for knowing to be that they, are disreputable characters, and their statements are positively denied on oath by the respondent. He puts his oath against theirs; and, on reading the evidence, I am forced to the conclusion that it is very doubtful indeed whether this man ought to be found guilty under the circumstances. It is a very serious thing to divorce anybody, much more serious, I think, than many of us suppose, and has a bad effect on the country. We are in the habit of letting these Bills go through this House simply because the Senate has passed them. 1 am probably as guilty as any one in that respect. We do not pay one-quarter of the attention to them that we ought to do, or contemplate the seriousness of what we do. Here is a man with three children who call him father, who is entitled to their respect if he is innocent of this charge, but who, if this Bill passes, will be deprived of his rights as a father, as well as his rights as a husband, and who will be disgraced in a very serious way. I suppose most of us would rather serve a term in the penitentiary than be under the disgrace that this man will be under if we pass this Bill. We must treat this case as one requiring substantial and strict proof. There is no evidence on which any judge or any intelligent jury would convict this man of the offence charged against him. I have not been approached by anybody or been asked to oppose this Bill. This is my own action as a legislator, and I say that if we grant this divorce on such evidence as we have here, we shall open the door to a most terrible state of affairs. There is not a respectable man in this Dominion who will not be subject to blackmail and the worst sort of treatment if this evidence is held to be sufficient. There have been similar cases to this one, but corroborative evidence has always been required. This is a case in which two accomplices of the very worst character, upon their own evidence, have induced the Senate to assume that this man is guilty. He denies their statements under oath, comes nil the way from British Columbia for the purpose, cross-examines these witnesses ; and we must come to the conclusion that his story is more likely to be true than theirs. No intelligent jury ever convicts a man of a crime on the evidence of accomplices ; and if they would, they would always be charged by the judge that such evidence must be corroborated. This is a serious matter, not only for this man, but for everybody in this country. I am pro-

bably less favourable to divorces than many: people:	I recognize, however, that there
are cases in which divorces should be granted under our laws, but they are extreme cases, and should admit of no doubt.( In the absence of the Chairman of the PriJ vate Bills Committee, who considered this Bill, and also of the Minister of Justice,; who, I think, should look into it, I would move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: This is a very unusual course to take on a Bill of this kind. I admit that the evidence, like the evidence in all cases upon which we grant divorces, is not of the very highest character. This case has been tried by the Senate, who examined the witnesses and had an opportunity of hearing their evidence, and who unanimously came to the decision that the case was proven, and reported the Bill to us. Not only have we the evidence of these persons, but we have the conduct of this man, of whom my hon. friend speaks as a very exemplary husband-a mail who left his wife and three little children and went off to British Columbia, where he remained for fourteen or sixteen years, and who, on his own evidence, in that time did not give ?400 to support them.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: They were not needing money.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext:
If they had needed money, they would not have got it from him. I do not know this woman at all, but I have it from the very best persons in the country that she is one of the most respectable women in the whole district, and the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Christie) is aware of that fact. She has raised three children, now grown to manhood, without any help from her husband. They are a most highly respected family, and I do not think any man, on reading the evidence, could fail to come to the conclusion that the Senate was perfectly right in unanimously passing this Bill. Any man who would leave his wife and family for sixteen years and let them drift as best they could, is no father and no man at all, and should not receive any consideration from this House.
Mi\ LANCASTER. Supposing this man did what the hon. gentleman alleges, that is no-ground for divorce; and it is quite clear on the evidence that his money was not needed because she returned the sums he sent her and did not want to have anything to do with him. There must be some reason why this woman, who has been wedded all these years, should want to get rid of her husband now, and we ought not to undo a marriage for the purpose of letting her marry again unless there are beyond question proper grounds for a divorce. The woman returned the money this man sent her. she returned the $100 payments, and there is no evidence that she suffered
for want of his money. The charge made by the hon. gentleman against this man is one we should not listen to. We are not here as judges granting alimony to this woman. What my hon. friend alleges would be a reason why a judge might decree judicial separation and grant alimony, but we are asked to absolutely divorce this man from his wife and children, and we are asked to do it on the evidence of two most disreputable characters, whom he contradicts on his o.ath. I cannot see what objection my hon. friend can have to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fitzpatrick) looking into the evidence and passing upon it before we come to a decision. This House is not going to prorogue to-morrow or next day, and the Minister of Justice will have plenty opportunity to see whether the position I take is a sound one. My hon. friend's desire for undue haste would rather indicate that the view I take is the right one. I am willing to have delay until the Minister of Justice looks into the matter. Surely my hon. friend can trust the Minister of Justice; and if the minister is convinced that I am wrong, then the Bill will pass.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is very anxious to have the opinion of the Minister of Justice when it suits his purpose ; but I notice that when the Minister of Justice does given an opinion, my hon. friend is not disposed to follow it. Another allegation he makes is that this woman returned $100 which her husband sent her. True she did, but the fellow never sent it to her until proceedings had been commenced for a divorce. It was only then that he sent her any money and he had deliberately refused to send her any for years previously. Why, the admissions of this man himself as to the company he kept and the places he visited and his general conduct corroborate the evidence given by his wife. How are you going to contradict the evidence given by other witnesses ? You will not get any respectable woman to give evidence as to the places this man frequented, and those who did, knew nothing about Mrs. McDer-mot and never saw her and gave their evidence in a straightforward manner. Of course the husband denies it, but he also denies Mrs. McDermot's evidence. The only witness he brought are two brothers-in-law of his own, and they testified that he was a very nice young boy when growing up, and one of them admits that the point on which he was brought to testify-that is with reference to Mrs. McDermot-occurred twenty odd years ago and he could not remember anything about it. I have no interest in the Bill other than that it was placed in my hands, and I have the best authority for believing that this woman is one of the most respectable in the whole country and raised a nice respectable family. Under the circumstances, I do not ' think there should be any hesitation in

granting her divorce from this man who deserted her.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext:
The request of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) is, it seems to me, under the circumstances, exceedingly reasonable. It will be five or six weeks, perhaps two months, perhaps more before prorogation takes place, so that there will be ample time to have the evidence thoroughly reviewed by officers of the government competent to give a judicial opinion upon it, and therefore I do not see why my hon. friend from Centre York, (Mr. Campbell) should object to the request made by the hou. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster). It is of the last importance that we should exercise the greatest care before pronouncing a dissolution of the marriage tie. Canadians, I believe, are a righteous and moral people, who desire that the moral foundations, which are the basis of a good and God fearing nation, should be strengthened ; and if we should exercise the haste urged upon the committee by my hon. friend from Centre York (Mr. Campbell), we would be aiming a blow at the very basis of those Christian principles which should govern our divorce pro ceedings and would in that way be inflict-* ing a blow on public morality.
I have looked at the evidence in this case. I am a lawyer and so is my hon. friend from Lincoln. I have had some experience in the dissection of evidence both in civil and criminal proceedings, and the hon. member for Centre York, while he is a man of great shrewdness and great business sagacity, is not accustomed to the dissection of evidence, to the careful analysis and weighing' of evidence, to ascertain what is sufficient to satisfy the burden of proof in a civil or criminal case. The hon. member for Centre ' York must bear this in mind that before! the decree can be passed in a case of this kind there must be not only evidence of guilt of the legal infidelity which is charged, but there must be overwhelming evidence of that guilt, there must be such evidence of that guilt as would satisfy the ordinary mind that the presumption of innocence is entirely overcome. My hon. friend from Lincoln reminds me of the principle that the evidence should go further, that it should satisfy the minds of the members of the committees of the two Houses through which the Bill is obliged to pass, that there is no reason able doubt at all about the innocence of the person charged with this grave offence. Before we dissect the particular facts which have been referred to, let us look at the procedure, the very admirable procedure which is one which makes for the protection of all classes and for the presex-vation of a high standard of morality in the state. The evidence as well as the Bill come down from the higher chamber to this House. For what purpose ? Surely for the very purpose referred to by my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), that every member of this Mr. CAMPBELL.
House, as is his duty, is to read that evidence and if he thinks it falls short of the remedy sought in this preamble he should have an opportunity of stating, as the hon. member for Lincoln does now, that in his opinion the evidence does fall short of that and that the committee ought to go slowly. The hon. member for Centre York (Mr. Campbell) has not that legal knowledge, that legal capacity of weighing evidence-I do not profess to be superior in that respect, I do not profess to have that business sagacity and shrewdness which characterize my hon. friend from Centre York (Mr. Campbell)- but I do say that it is my opinion that there might be a good deal stronger evidence in this case and yet the committee might hesitate before coming to the conclusion that the grave charge made has been fully upheld. Now to show that the hon. member for Centre York is pursuing a wrong line of argument in this case I -would point out to you that the line that he has taken does not touch, except in one or two minor instances, the root of the charge as recited in this preamble. My hon. friend has referred only to the questions of legal cruelty and desertion, facts which are not grounds for the granting of any divorce in this country, and which are not set forth in the Bill either. They are merely evidence of collateral circumstances, evidence which might well have been excluded by the committee, but evidence which certainly, taken alone, cannot have any weight whatever with respect to the matter under consideration by the committee of the Senate.
The fact that the witnesses are of the same disreputable class is surely a circumstance to be taken into consideration. Surely it is not the intention and is not to be the principle laid down by this committee in this case that whatever evidence comes down from the Senate is to be passed by every member of this committee as absolute and undoubted evidence of the guilt of the accused. Surely we have functions to perform, the responsibility of which we cannot shirk and if we say that upon that evidence there is a doubt then I say it is our duty to face that question boldly and investigate and if there be a question then surely no person can be hurt by the very reasonable request of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) to refer the evidence with the Bill to the Minister of Justice asking him to consider the matter and make a report in this case, so that dissection and discussion of the details is not necessary in this committe but we may have the report of the law officer of the Crown, a gentleman skilled in that work who will give the committee the benefit of his judgment, a judicial judgment and cue which cannot fail to enlighten the committee one way or the another. It would be futile and I think unpleasant to discuss this matter in committee here, nor would it be pleasant or serve any good result, but to refer the evidence with the Bill back to the

Minister of Justice and to ask his opinion and to ask him to lay his report before the House would be a step in the right direction and be travelling along safe ground and on safe lines.	.
