The hon. gentleman has said that there is a good case in his opinion against this man. I am going to talk for a minute or two as I would to a jury if I were defending this man. Just see what we are coming to. Against this man appear two most disreputable characters who for years have been living on the proceeds of their vice. They say so themselves. There is no defamation in saying that because it is their own statement. That is the way they qualify themselves as witnesses ; in fact, it is the way they qualify themselves as experts in this case. These are the only people who state anything against this man. They are bad characters on their admission, the most disreputable characters to have in the country, women of the most vicious kind, women who are dangerous to any community, breaking the law every day of their lives and liable to go to prison if they can be convicted and if the authorities are smart enough to prosecute them. On their own statement they have been guilty day after day of having led an immoral life. That is their character. Talk about their character being as good as his.. He does not admit that he is that kind of man. On the contrary, he denies it. He is backed up by the fact that he is a respectable merchant doing business in a community where these people are drawn from on behalf of thii
200J

woman, who for some strange reason wants to get a divorce from her lawful husband. In that same town she could have found dozens of men to swear to the bad character of this man if it were so. If she had called, that kind of evidence, if she had brought respectable people before the committee of the Senate, I could have listened with some patience if they had stated that his character was not as good as theirs. But, she does not do it, she does not bring a witness to show that this man is not to be believed on oath, but he puts into the box two men of the highest character, clergymen, who swear to what he was when he was a young man, and one of whom was out there in the place at the time he was supposed to have committed this offence with these outrageously disreputable women. Where is the excuse for the hon. gentleman saying that one's character is as good as the other ? Where is the protection for any respectable man who is not always surrounded by three or four witnesses able to prove an alibi ? What is the proposition of the hon. member for Centre York?-that if he was not guilty he should have proved it by some one else. Can the hon. gentleman prove where he was a year and two months and a day ago yetster-day ? Can he prove where he was fifteen mouths ago on a certain Wednesday at eight o'clock in the evening ? It is all very well to say he should have done it ? Could my hon. friend do anything else but what this man has done ? If any one made a false charge against my hon. friend such as that which has been made against this man could my hon. friend have done anything else but what this man has done ? We have to take this thing seriously. We have as much right to suppose that this evidence was given against yourself, Mr. Speaker, or myself, or the hon. member for Centre York and ask ourselves what we, absolutely innocent, would do or expect in the face of that evidence. What could we do but tell the truth as this man has done? If he were guilty would he come all the way down here from British Columbia without counsel and pledge his oath as he has done? If he were guilty of perjury he could be convicted on the evidence of these same two witnesses.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: Why does he not prosecute these women ?

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext:
What earthly good would that be to the poor man after he was divorced ? A lot of satisfaction it would be, after a man is taken away from his wife and children, and after he and his children are disgraced for ever, to prosecute these outrageously disreputable women. When the honourable and learned Judge Britton was a member of this House he introduced ti Bill providing that divorces should be granted by the courts of the land and not by parliament. As I was personally not in favour Mr. LANCASTER.
of divorces, I took no part in the discussion on that Bill, but if we are going to grant divorces in such cases as this, then by all means let us have divorce courts which will decide these matters judicially and on sound principles. My hon. friend from Centre York (Mr. Campbell) might have disposed of this matter according to my suggestion, but perhaps he forgot that by the rules of the House we will only have to prevail on him for three minutes longer in order that we may have a wider opportunity for discussing this matter and getting the Minister of Justice to throw some light on it, as the committee must then rise anyway.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: It is evident you want light.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend may be in a great hurry to divorce this wife, Clara Bidwell McDermot, from her husband, George Burton McDermot ; he may think it is a very wise thing to rush this legislation through, but I say again, as I said fifty minutes ago, that the consideration of this Bill should stand over until we have the opinion of the law officers of the Crown. I trust that even at this late hour, even now when the hour for private Bills is about to expire, he will accept my suggestion. I do not want to be unduly contentious with my hon. friend (Mr. Campbell), and I trust he will consent that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again. If he will not consent, then so long as the lamp holds out to burn we will endeavour to bring pressure on him. He says we should not shirk the responsibility, but that is exactly what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) is doing. He is endeavouring to shirk the responsibility by rushing this Bill through without allowing the House to seriously consider the matter.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: You want to shirk the responsibility and throw it on the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Campbell) has no right to say that. If I wanted to shirk my responsibility I could remain silent and let the Bill pass, but I assume the responsibility of pointing out what I think is wrong in this Bill.

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext: If you are opposed to it, vote agaihst it; why do you want to talk it out ?

subtopic: RELIEF OF CLARA BID WELL McDERMOT.
speechtext:
I suppose the hon. gentleman thinks it is all right for a member to vote for or against a Bill and not give his reasons. There are gentlemen on the other side of the House who may think that good policy, but on this side even so much of a back bencher as the member for Lincoln thinks it right to state the reasons why he opposes a measure. It may be supposed that I oppose this Bill because I am not in favour of divorces, but, Sir, I recog-

raze that the statutes of Canada require us to grant divorces in proper eases, and, so long as that is the law of the land, I will vote for divorces in proper cases. But this is not a proper case, in my opinion, because the preamble of the Bill states that about the month of April, 1901, this man did certain things, and it declares that the petitioner has proved the allegations in her petition. In my judgment, that preamble is not borne out by the evidence.
The hour for private Bills having expired, the House resumed in Committee of Supply.
St. Lawrence river and canals-reducing shoals west of Cornwall, $5,000.
['After private Bills we hope to proceed with the Autonomy Bill.']
Where are these shoals, and how much altogether will it require to do the work ?

speakeroldname: Hon. H. R. EMMBRSON (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
The work consists in dredging shoals, one opposite Hooper's creek, one mile west of Cornwall, dnd the other opposite Archibald's point, about one and a-half miles west at the head of the canal and connected with the mainland. The contract was entered Into with W. J. Poupore & Company. This $5,000 is required to pay off the contract, the whole contract being for $30,500.
Mr. HAGGARfT.. ,Is this the first expenditure on it ?	'
Yes. A contract was let last year, whan an amount wals voted towards the work, and this is the balance to close up the contract.
How much has been expended on the contract ?

It is estimated that there 'Will be expended up to the 30th of June $80,500, and that will complete the work. In the main estimates o!f 1904-5 we had $25,500, which left the balance of $5,000,
Rapide Plat canal-enlargement of upper entrance, $4,200.
'Mr. EMiMiBRSON. This completesi the work.
What is the total amount ?

'The final estimate for the whole Work was $81,500. There wag paid up to the 30th of November, 1904, $19,063.40. That left a balance due of $2,437.52, which, added to the drawback of $1,268.53 makes $3,705.05, which with the engineer's staff salaries, $500, makes $4,200.
Who are the contractors ?

Gilbert was the contractor. The original contract was let in 1900. There rwere three tenders, and Mr. Gilbert's was the lowest.
Soulanges canal-steel bridge at power house, $500 ; construction, $36,500 ; total, $37,000.

The $500 is to cover the additional cost of the superstructure. $4,000 was voted In the main estimates, and the total cost will be $4,500. The $36,500 is a balance due to Manning & Macdonald, who had a contract for construction. The contractors are making claims against the department, hut this is all that the department recognizes.

What was Manning & Macdonald's total contract ?
Mr. EMMEiRSION. The total payments on the 13th section to the 31st of December, 1904, amounted- to $682,407.75, -that is covering a period of years. The alnount remaining unpaid is $34,182.52, making the total amount about $717,000.
Will the minister tell us how that compares with the estimated cost by the department when the contract was entered into ?
This is in excess of the original estimate.
Ho'w much ?
My engineer cannot give me that amount.
Is it more than double?
Somewhere in the vicinity of $50,000.

It must be more than that. The amount expended on this contract is in the neighbourhood of $720,000. That would leave the estimated cost by the department $670,000. It would be interesting to the House to see how near the actual cost of 'construction came to the estimate by the engineers.

(I have not got that information, and my chief engineer tells me he does not remember what' the original estimate was. It was an estimate made many years ago, 'I am not personally familiar with it, but in the judgment of one of the 'officials the cost was' between $50,000 and $60,000 in excess of the original estiJ mate.

I suppose the hon. gentleman would not object to furnishing that estimate at a later date ?
Mr. BMMiERi&ON. Certainly not.
Welland canal-to deepen portion of long level, $52,000.

How it is that the estimate was exceeded this' year ?
M*r. BMMERSON. It was estimated that we would expend about $150,000 this year, hut the contractors made greater progress than estimated and it requires $52,000 to continue the work and pay the drawback up to the end of the current year. It is

estimated that the two months' 'work will amount to $25,000 for each month, and there is a drawback of $10,000, making $60,000 in all. We have on hand $8,000 of the $150,000, so that the amount required is $52,000.
Does this finish it ?

With what is in the main estimates, this item of $52,000 Will finish the whole contract, so my chief engineer informs met
' Mr. HAGGAET. How much will you have in your lowest water navigation on the long level ?
At normal level we will have seventeen feet.
But at low water ?
Fifteen feet.
That is a foot deeper than the navigation on the locks ?
Yes.
What do you make the total expenditure on that ?
That does not cover all the expenditure in' deepening the long level?
No, there was expended up to the 31st December, 1904, $390,270 on this long level.
Then this is an expenditure of $700,000 for the purpose of putting this level to what it ought to have been originally when built ?

With the amount to be expended?
Mr. BMMIERSO'N. About $540,000.
When will the work be completed ?

This is supposed to complete the work within this fiscal year.
Trent canal-to complete survey, $25,000 ; damages by flooding, $7,000 ; $32,000.
Will the minister give us a concise account of the two different lmes-the survey line to Port Hope and the line following the Trent river down, and which he thinks is the most advantageous ?

We have surveyed three lines, one to Cobourg, one to Port Hope the other to Trenton. The final report giving a comparison of the different routes has not been received. The work is not yet completed. In order to meet the liabilities incurred during this current year, we will require $25,000 for the surveys on the Trent Valley system. I am not in a position to give to the committee even the judgment of the engineer, in consequence of Mr. EMMERSON.
the survey not being completed and a final report not having been made. This matter was started by the department with an open mind, and I hope to have an exhaustive and thorough report from the independent engineer-a gentleman of eminence in his profession-and as soon as that report is received, H shall lay it on the table.
How much has been expended on the survey thus far ?
Up to the 1st April, $16,259.	[DOT]

I should judge that the hon. minister has had the reports of his own engineers on the different routes ; and there has been a survey of that portion of the canal which was' intended to suit the people in North York. What was the result of that survey ?

I have not the report from the engineer. We have had reports in the department with respect to the different routes, and these have been laid before parliament from time to time. This has not been laid before parliament. There was a general complaint on the part of the different parties interested or the different' committees that, these surveys were not exhaustive in all instances, and I have even heard it alleged by hon. members in this House that sometimes the engineers who had made these surveys did not do so with an open mind, that they were biased and I promised the House last session that a survey would be made by engineers who would stand entirely indifferent as respects the different communities or localities interested, and in pursuance of that promise tins survey was commenced. I am not in a position to furnish the House with the information inasmuch as the report has not been presented as the work is not completed.

There is in the department the report of the engineer in charge of the Trent canal who had surveyed both routes, and his report was strongly in favour of the Bay of Quinte or Trenton route. The minister has had no report since that from the engineer in charge of the canal ?
The report from the independent engineer has not yet come in.
Is an engineer at present employed by the government for the purpose ?
Yes, Mr. Watt was employed to survey the proposed routes, the Port Hope route, the Cobourg route, the Trenton route and at the other end, the Simcoe-Georgian bay route and the Aurora route.
Have you had any report on the Aurora route ?
Not yet; there is no final report as to the result of the surveys.
When will the other' lift lock he finished to enable them to get into the waters of Lake Simeoe ?
It will be completed for the opening of navigation next season.
Then there is to be continuous navigation for what length, the whole of Lake Simeoe and down to where V
Down below Peterborough to Rice lake.
When were the surveys authorized by the government to Cobourg and Port Hope ?
At the last session when a vote of parliament was asked.
I suppose you had come to a decision before you asked for money to survey these routes.
To make all possible surveys and take into consideration the whole question, to furnish such evidence as would be of Value in finally determining the route to be adopted.
With reference to the November campaign had Mr. Aylesworth any authority from the department to tell the people in the riding that the Trent Valley canal would go through Port Hope ?

I was not even aware that Mr. Aylesworth made any such statement. I might mention also that my attention was called by the hon. member for East Northumberland (Mr. Cochrane) to the possibility of a route by Brighton and I gave instructions to have that investigated and if it was found at all feasible to have it surveyed.

I think that now the elections are all over the department might accept the opinion that was given by the engineer in charge, that there is no doubt whatever that the only practicable and feasible route is the Trenton route, and that you should use all the money you have on it in the construction of the canal instead of spending it on useless surveys.

I have no doubt my hon. friend is sincere but I have heard words uttered by my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Ward) who is not, I am sorry to see, in his place, that are entirely contrary to the views expressed by my hon. friend. There are differences of opinion and I should hope to have such information placed before me as would enable me to form some judgment of my own and I shall be very pleased to coincide with either my hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) or the hon. gentleman from Durham (Mr. Ward).
I am .only forming my opinion on the engineer's report.
When does the minister expect a report of these surveys ?

We ask in the main estimates $24,000 and we are now asking to complete $12,000. This amount is to cover the payment of drawback, increase in quantities and extra work for Cote St. Paul and Brewster's bridges. There was an Increase, the bulk of it on earth excavation. The material was found to be of a very unfavourable nature. There was also an increase in the amount of cribwork. A portion of last year's vote lapses. This work was done by contract, Quinlan & Robertson are the contractors. This completes the work. One of these bridges is at Cote St. Paul, and the other called Brewster's bridge. They both replace old bridges.
What is the object of separating vote 51 from vote 53, seeing that they both refer to the Lachine canal?
One is capital, the other is current expenses.
Give us gome idea of the extent of the enlargement of the canal?
These were bridges across the Lachine canal, new bridges replacing old ones that had become decayed, and the opening was widened.
The words are ' enlargements and improvements.'
That was for widening and opening the canal. This work is done by contract.
How much does the cost exceed the estimate of the department when the contract was entered into?
The total expenditure in connection witlr this work up to the 1st of April, was $15S,882. We are asking for $12,000 more. I have not the exact figures, but there was some excess.
The contract was based upon a lot of items.

It was a schedule contract. There were two contracts, both relating to bridges. One contract was let to Quinlan & Robertson, that is the one at C6te St. Paul bridge, and the other was let to John Quinlan. The excess over the estimate was about $12,000 on the two contracts, and that was largely due to the character of the excavation.
The bridge at C6te St. Paul was an ordinary wooden bridge, has it been changed into a steel bridge ?
Yes.
Are there two locks at C6te St. Paul, or only one ? Was the old one enlarged ?
The old one was enlarged and the span was increased in consequence. The old bridge was necessarily a shorter bridge, and in consequence of the enlargement the old lock had to be increased in length.
Does the minister know what is the size of the new lock made where the old lock was? Is it large enough to receive ocean vessels, as it was proposed to make it ?
They are now 270 feet in length, and they were 245 feet. The depth of water is 14 feet on the mitre sill.
Was that contract let by tender ?

Yes. It is a schedule contract, and is work that necessarily had to be done in the interest of the canal. The estimated cost of the whole work when these two slope walls are finally completed is $235,000. But this work has necessarily to be done within a very short time while the canal Is unwatered, in the spring. So much is done each season. It is done by tender and contract, and the lowest tender has been accepted in all cases.
That must have been done during the last month when the water was out of the canal.
My hon. friend is right.
How is it that there was not enough money to finish it?
We are only asking for $13,000 during this year.
That is additional to the amount in the main estimates.
In the main estimates it was $13,000. It was expected that we might not do very much during this year but the conditions were favourable and* we instructed them to do the work.
What is the total amount ?
Will that complete the work ?	-
No ; it will go on for five or six years. A -certain proportion of the canal will be sloped each year under the specifications.
It is only at the locks it is sloped with cut stone ?
It is all along the whole bank of the canal.
It is not all done in cut stone ?
It is not cut stone ; it is dry masonry and rip-rapping.
Is it done by the yard ?
By the cubic yard.
How much is it by the cubic yard ?
For dry masonry $5.50, and for rip-rap repairing $2.40.
Is this season's work finished ?

That portion that is ordinarily under water is attended to when the canal is unwatered in the spring, and from now until the 1st of July that which is above water will be attended to. The total estimated cost of that during this current year is $45,000. We only took an appropriation in the main estimates for $13,000, and therefore we are asking for the balance for the current fiscal year of $32,-
000.
How can work of that kind be done by contract ? I understand that it is generally done by the employees of the government and those who work on the canal.
No.
How can you carry on the work for five or six years by contract ?
They tender at schedule prices, so much per cubic yard for concrete, so much per cubic yard for dry masonry and so much for rip-rapping.
It is always the same contractor ?
This is the first work that these gentlemen have done.
This year ?
Yes ; the contract was let -some time last summer.
To be done this spring?
A certain portion of it to be done this spring, and next year there will be another portion of it done.
Was not most of this work done when the canal was constructed ?
This work became necessary by reason of the deepening of the canal. When they deepened the canal the old work was destroyed ; it broke down.
This is renewal work ?
Practically renewal work caused by the deepening of the canal.
How is the work standing where it was put in after the canal was deepened ?
It is standing very well, so the chief engineer says.
How long is it since tile Lachine canal was deepened ?
About nine years.
Has this work been going on ever since ?
No ; there has been a *certain proportion of this work going on since then. Delormier had the contract.
I understand Delormier was furnishing the stone. He had a quarry.
His contract was for the other as well. He had to furnish the stone because he had a contract for the other.
On what part of the canal ?
Between CSte St. Paul and Lachine.
Is that part finished ?
That part is not finished. The south side has not been touched.
It may be kept on like that for ten years more.
It would be a pretty large sum if we expended it all at one time, but it will perfect the canal to have the work done.
It . costs $15,000 this year, and it will be about the same thing next year.
I think that for the work that was let under contract to Quinlan & Robertson it is estimated that the total will be about $235,000. They are doing $-15,000 worth of it this year.
That means about five years ?
Yes.
Is this rip-rapping from the top of the rock excavation, or does it go down to the bottom ?
It goes down to the bottom.
Rip-rapping at the bottom where it is in rock excavation ?
The work is only a few feet on the top.
They lay a concrete foundation in the bottom where there is rock, and this is in order to sustain the slope of the sides above.

Rip-rapping at the side of the canal generally commences from the top of the rock excavation. There is a great deal of rock excavation on the Lachine canal, and if the rip-rapping was put in properly the deepening of the canal would not affect the rip-rap at all.
As a matter of fact, I am informed that it did affect it, and that it fell down.

It should not have done so. You can deepen down the prism of the canal and the rip-rapping should only commence from the top of the rock work. It must have been very badly done, or there must have been something wrong about it, because the rip-rapping should never go down to the bottom of the rock excavation. It should only commence at the top. It is extremely curious. To my knowledge, a lot of the excavation for the Lachine canal is in rock, and that the rip-rapping should go down to the bottom is impossible. Riprapping commences at the top of the prism or of the rock excavation ; and if it were put in properly, the deepening of the canal would not interfere with it at all.

As I understand it, in some places it was found to be necessary. In other places it only goes from the top of the rock excavation, as my hon. friend very properly says. In all cases where it was possible to do it in that way it was done. The chief engineer tells me that in certain places it was -found to be necessary to go to the bottom and to lay a concrete foundation.
Cornwall' canal-to purchase and fit up concreting apparatus, $2,400.
What do you want this on the Cornwall canal for?
It Is for all the St. Lawrence canals from Prescott to Cornwall. The total estimated cost Is $6,230 and we previously voted $4,100.
Does that include a crushing apparatus?
A boiler, engine, stone crusher, concrete mixer, two derricks with engines and the erection and installation.

It will cost as much to remove it from one place to another as to do the work.
' Lachine canal-underpinning wall, basin No.
2, $10,000.
This wall was falling in and the work can only be done when the canal is unwatered. The estimate was $17,000 ; wre took a vote of $7,000 and we ask for the balance.
What was the engineer's estimate for the whole work ?

$17,000 and we previously took $7,000 thinking we would only do that amount of work up to the end of the fiscal year, but it was found possible to complete the work. The officers of the department found, they were wrong as to their expectations.
Is the work completed now?
Yes.
How was the estimate of the department wrong?

The items are as follows : excavation, 2,000 yards at $1.15 per yard; concrete filling, 2,000 yards at $4.50 per yard; timber for supports, 2,000 lineal feet at 25 cents ; planking for facing, $416 ; cement, $4,000; engineering, $784; total, $17,000.	.
What has become of that timber?
The plank facing would be utilized and the timber for the supports would be in the stores of the canal.
It was a matter of complaint in the Curran bridge case that there was a great deal of timber used for the same purpose and it disappeared.
This might disappear iij the same way, but there are officials there to look after it and it will not disappear if they do their duty.
This $10,000 completes the work?

Yes, that winds it up.
Widening tail race-to pay contractor O. L. Henault for extra time, $514.60.
How is it that this poor contractor did not get paid ?

The total payment up to May 1, 1904, final estimate was $9,234.60. The contractors claimed a much larger amount than the vote, but the chief engineer allowed $514.60. The following are the items allowed by the chief engineer: cutting down and removing piers, $180; assisting government employees, $88.50 ; furnishing 34 yards of displacement, $45 ; supplying 22 tons of crushed stone, $24.80 ; supplying 22 tons of Potsdam stone, $33 ; iron, $53.80.
The appropriation is for extra time and according to your statement you are paying for work and material?
That must be a clerical error.
You had better change the wording of the item then.
We will change it to ' extra work.'
The engineer passed on this amount and decided it was correct?
Yes, but of course the contractor put in a claim for more.

I have no doubt about that; they generally ask more expecting to get less.
Improvements to flume on power house, $3,500.
What is this for?
This work is rendered necessary on account of the proposed operation of the locks by electric power. The present power will probably be sufficient to drive all the machinery.
Since when have the locks worked by electricity ?
We are only getting ready for that. This work is necessary to' enable us to do it.

When will that be in
operation ?
We hope very shortly, some of the gates will be fitted this summer, and all of them, we hope, by October.
When you have that work done, what are you going to do with the eight or ten men who are employed on nearly every lock ?
I do not know whether this will be a labour-saving machine or not. It may be necessary to dispense with the services of some of these gentlemen.
Does the use of electricity result in a saving in expense ?

It expedites the traffic. I will not say that it will be possible to dispense with the services of the men, because, while the vessels go through with greater expedition, they have to be guided in their passage, and men are necessary for that purpose.

On the Soulanges canal there are very few men employed, and with the electric system we could dispense with half the men employed on the Lachine canal to-day. Will this apply to the old locks or only to the new ?

If it is found to be a success, all the locks will be operated in the same way. I do not know that the use of electricity on the Soulanges canal* has obviated the necessity of having men. The experience there is that only expedition is obtained, and not a lessening of thes cost, because men have to be constantly! on the watch as the vessels pass through.
Lachine canal-lock gates, suspension, $4,500.
Mi1. EMMERSON. This is for changing the hanging gear of the locks. The present hanging or suspension apparatus is not satisfactory, in the judgment of the officials of the department, because it is very* easily put out of gear. Stone cutting of races, protection beams, and other necessary work will cost $3,000, and iron beams for the gates will cost $1,500. There are five locks to be gated. The system adopted is the same as is used on the Ottawa canal,-which is giving every satisfaction.
What has become of the invention of Mr. 'Manny ? Is it being put cm every gate ?
It is being put on many.

Has it been found1 a success ?
iMr. EMMERSON. That 5s what the officers say.
Is it to lock the gates after they are shut ?
It is it)o protect them' from vessels knocking against them.
In going down ?
Going up.
Do the vessels do anj harm to the gates ?
They do a great deal. We had an experience on the Welland canal where three gates were sent to glory.

Was the vessel going up ?
IMr. EMMERSON. Yes.
If that improvement had been on those gates, would the acciJ dent have happened ?
The chief engineer thinks that while it might not absolutely prevent accidents, accidents will be less likely to happen.
Would it be good policy to put it on every gate ?

We are trying the experiment on the Eachine canal first and then will consider the advisability of asking a vote to put it on all the canals.
TO complete paving of Mill street, $2,200.
How much does that cost altogether ?

Besides this amount V
Mr. EMMERiSON. Yes, the total Will he over $50,000.
Mr.. ARMSTRONG. Will this complete the work ?	'
Yes.
Is this on government property ?

Yes, the government owns Mill Street.
Chambly canal-culvert St. Theresa Island, $2,500 ; culvert at.Deneau's farm, $2,000, $4,500.
Is this a new culvert or repairing an old one ?

This is a culvert on St. Theresa island, Iroquois river. There
were culverts there before. The total expenditure is $12,383. If was let by contract to ,a man named Finn, but he did not complete his contract, and the canal staff have been obliged to complete it.
You charged it against him ?
Yes.
Will that complete the whole thing ?
Yes.
What is the (Cost of the culvert at Denean's farm ?
We expended $3,059 in 1904, and are asking now $2,000 more. The! total cost will be about $10,000.
What is this for ?

It is for the purpose! of carrying a stream under the canal.
St. Ours landing wharf, $4,500.
This is a renewal of a landing wharf below the locks, which has been in existence a very long time, and1 requires to be renewed. We require $4,500 to complete. The amount voted before was $6,000.
How is it your engineers get so far astray in their estimates'(
The superintendent engineer reports that a certain amount off work can he done which is larger than was, expected, and on his report we ask fox' a vote.
Will that complete the whole tiling ?
Yes.
Is the minister sure he did not promise, when he got the vote for $6,000 that that would complete the! work ?
Speaking from general custom, I would say I did not. But if the question were asked at all, I would' have asked my chief engineer and no doubt' would have answered just as he told me.
If the minister made' the statement that $0,000 would complete and it is costing $10,000-

I would apologize on the spot.
Trent canal-completion of work of lowering floor of lock, $2,500.
Is this in connection with the new lift-lock?
This is the lock below Peterborough which was built when I the canal was originally built.
That would be about seventy years ago. Is this one of the old locks that is now owned by the Ontario government ? Is it one of the locks not conveyed to the Ontario government.
Yes. This is right at the town of Peterborough.

Will this render this lock available for the present system of navigation proposed on the Trent canal?
Mi\ EMMERSON. That is the object of it.
To complete new dam at Peterborough lock,
This is to complete the new dam. The work is let by contract to a Mr. Burnet. $2,955 was expended up to the 31st of December, 1904, and this is to complete it. We asked $7,000.
This $2,000 will complete it?
Yes.
What is the total cost?
To pay claim Geo. Matthews Company for damage caused by water, $600.

This amount is to pay a firm at Peterborough damages for injury to their goods caused by the raising of the waters of the Otonabee river in consequence of the government's works in building a new dam at Whitlaw's rapids. The cellars were flooded and a quantity of fertilizing material and bacon damaged. The claim was investigated by the engineer and was substantiated by his report. The matter was referred to the Justice Department, and they advised a settlement and it was deemed advisable to pay the price demanded rather than have litigation in view of the opinion of -the Department of Justice.

One would think that the engineers in building the dam would know what damage would be caused above it and would have advised the people to remove the goods.
St. -Peter's canal-dredging, $1,500.
Is this contract let by tender and if so, what is the price per yard?

No, it is not by tender. This is down in Gape Breton where it is almost impossible to get a dredge. There are none there and we had to convey one from Sydney. We paid so much per day for the dredge which we got from the Dominion Coal Company and the conveyance and cost of the work has certainly exceeded the estimates made by the engineers.
Do you pay for the towing?
Yes.
How much?

There is a dispute. We paid $68 a day for the dredge ; that included the towing.
Mi-. ARMSTRONG. Can the minister give us an idea of the amount of material that was moved by this dredge?
No, we have no such estimate.
Was the price so much an hour?
So much per day.
What is the depth and length of the clay that was removed ?
There were two shoals at the St. Peter's canal which obstructed its navigation.
What was the extent of it?
There were about $3,000 to $4,000 expended.
Is the department satisfied that the work is done properly?

Yes, the only dispute is as to the time occupied in taking the dredge from Sydney to the canal. There is a dispute as to the number of days. The work was- necessary in the fall of the year and they contended that the time occupied in transporting the dredge should be included, the ten days occupied in that way. It was finally settled, the officers of tlie department agreeing upon the matter ; it will cost, including the towing, about $3,500.
The amount you got last year was $2,000.
Yes, we are asking more.
Who has the work?
It was under the supervision of the man who had charge of the canal. The Dominion Coal Company rented the dredge.
Was the Dominion Coal Company the owner of the dredge?
Yes.
And the department paid the coal company?
The work was done under the instruction of Mr. Devereaux. He is an official of the department, and has charge of that.
Was the work last year done under the same conditions ?
This was all done last year.
Was there any advertising for tenders ?	[DOT]
There is nothing in the shape of a dredge there at all, the nearest dredge would he in the city of St. John. The government have no dredge at their disposal.
That would be the converse case to the Port Arthur case, where there were dredges and nowhere else, and no advertisements were published.

Inquiries were made. This work was very urgent, navigators were making complaints, and the officials of the department had instructions from me to make inquiries in all directions to see what could be done towards getting a dredge to do this work. We could not find a dredge in any of the departments, and we were finally obliged to take this dredge at Sydney belonging to the Dominion Coal Company.
Carillon and Grenville canal-guide piers, $1,017.

These guide piers are at the head of these two canals. The contract was let in 1901 to Martineau Sons & Le-moine. The work is completed. The amount of the contract was $19,788.55, and this Is a balance to complete.
Is this for extras ?
No ; it is a part of the contract.
It is a wonder you did not ask for the amount last year to finish the contract.
I will explain. These contractors had a claim in the department, this balance was in dispute, and this amount was finally adjusted by the chief engineer.
This is over and above the contract ?

No, it is included in the contract; but the contractors made a greater claim. In the final estimate they put in claims, as a rule, for more work, and there is always a dispute as to the quantity. A dispute arose in connection with this contract, and it was finally adjusted by the chief engineer, and under his certificate $1,017 was agreed upon.
Welland canal-to pay Stephen Vanderburg for time lost, Injured while on duty, two-thirds time, 196 days at $1.75 per day, $228.86.
This man was engaged at the Port Maitland lock and was injured by falling into the lock, on the 6th of August last, and is still laid, up in consequence.
What was the special work he was employed at ?
They were repairing the floor of the lock while it was unwatered.
Was it because of any negligence of bis fellow-servants, or was it his own fault ?

I believe it has been the custom for years to give indemnities in similar cases. The matter was submitted to me, and, in view of the course that had been followed, I decided to ask for a vote of parliament for the amount. I am not acquainted with the details, I could not say just what kind of work he was doing, or as to whose fault it was.

I am not finding fault with this, but I just wish to know the policy of the government, if, when a man is injured while at his work, they pay an indemnity without bothering to inquire, like an uncharitable corporation would, as to whether it was his fault or the fault of somebody else.

We do not pay. We inquire and then submit the matter to parliament. This has not been paid. It cannot be paid until parliament votes the amount. Of course, as I understand it, the custom has been to look into each individual case and if a man is injured on duty an allowance of a certain percentage is granted unless' it is the fault of the la-, bourer or workman. In that case it is not considered.	i
And there is no discrimination between Liberals and Conserva-vatives ?	.
No.
It is granted irrespective of whether there is negligence attributed to the government or not ?
It is granted if the man is not negligent.
If it is n mere accident ?
If it is a mere accident.

You do not consider it necessary to make out a prima facie casei?
Miscellaneous-salaries of extra clerks, copyists and messengers, other than those who have passed the Civil Service examination, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $1,000.
What is the total amount you have expended this year ?
Lachine canal-repairs, $10,205.
Where would these repairs be ?

These are several items that arose in connection with the working of the canal and the making of repairs for the season. I can give the dif-

ferent items. We replaced wooden by cast iron mooring posts on locks and approaches at a cost of $4,230.	i
That must be an unforeseen expenditure ?
These were repairs of which the department had not been advised at the time the main estimates were prepared.
How much was there In the main estimates for this work ?
Then that would be $65,000 instead of $55,000 ?
Yes.
What kind of repairs are these ?

In addition to the posts there were the following:	Underpinning crib at lower approach to lock 4, raising Wellington bridge, removing and renewing broken pivot, four 150 ton hydraulic jacks, four 25 ton hydraulic jacks for raiilsing large bridges, building line fence and sidewalks at Cote St. Paul, clearing site of Wellington basin leased to the Moorehouse Goal Company, removing dross and stone stored for repairs and concrete wall on the south side of the tail race of the waste weir at Cote St. Paul.
Mr. HAGO AItT. Is that our own waste weir or the 'waste weir from the mill ?

This is one of the waste weirs at Cote St. Paul in connection with the lock.
Beauharnois canal-repairs, $4,000.
Are the government going to keep that canal In operation ?

We have to keep it in operation. It is used to a certain extent and while it is not very important as a canal it seems to be necessary to keep it up. There are some water-powers on it. I have not bean able to reach the conclusion that the canal should be abolished as a canal.
Has my bon. friend been approached in regard to utilizing the water-powers on the Canal?

The matter has been up from time to time.. There have been applications made to the department from a good many sources, from eoi'porations and individuals, for water rights. I have not been able to determine the question or look into it as I would like to. I do not know what course should be pursued.
There are a few vessels passing through it. It is not a very costly work, as I understand, as there are very few men employed on it. It is important

,*
however to keep it in repair as long as it is not costly because I can see that before long, if the hon. gentleman examines the subject, he may come to the conclusion that it would be a good thing to grant the right to use the water-powers. It would be an immense water-power, because there is about 80 feet of a chute. The canal is not in operatioit to-day to any great extent but it requites to be kept in repair because otherwise it would go to decay very soon.
St. Peter's canal-repairs, $500.
Where is the other item for canals ?
Does my hon. friend want to discuss it now at this stage ? I expect to have it in the supplementaries for the coming year.

It may be discussed on the supplementaries for the coming year.
Farran's Point canal-to complete the acetylene gas plant, $300.
Surely you are not putting acetylene on this canal where you have so much power to generate electricity ?
This is isolated; this was done some time ago and the vote is to complete.
Why, two or three miles of wire would connect it with the other canals. It seems to be an absurd expenditure.
This was not done in my day.
Is it to light the canal?
Yes.
Then I would advise the minister to fling it out and to connect with wires from his electric plant.
I certainly will look into it; it is five miles from the Cornwall canal and about ten from the Ilapide Plat.

Has a gentleman named Painchaud, of Montreal, written to the Minister of Railways with regard to an invention he has for making acetylene gas
safer?
I have had several ap-lications respecting improvements, but I do not remember the names.
I understand that Mr. Painchaud's process will prevent the accidents which have recently occurred?

Application has been made to the department in connection with the lighting of ears on the Intercolonial Railway, stating that this improvement is better than Pintsch gas and that the Canadian Pacific Railway were installing it.

Welland canal-lowering head of lock No. 1,
What is the necessity for this work?

The breast wall and foundation at the head of lock No. 1, was originally built about one foot too high, and it requires to be lowered in order to
maintain fourteen feet navigation in the event of the retaining wall between the old and new canal giving out, as is very likely to happen at any time. The estimate is $10,000 and after the work is completed the retaining wall will not be required.
Is that the total amount?
That is the total estimated cost.
Did we not have a vote for this before ?
No.
This is down at Port Dalhousie. Is not the government spending money every year to keep that retaining wall in repair ?
We had to repair the retaining wall as long as it remained, but now we are going to abandon that wall.
How much per year has it cost to repair that retaining wall?
It is considerably out of repair now and before it gives out we want to do this work so as to obviate the necessity of any further repairs.
There are one or two items for the Department of Agriculture which I would like to get passed to-night.
We did a good night's work for the purpose of getting through at 11 o'clock, and the explanations of the Minister of Agriculture are generally so brief that he might keep us here till 1 o'clock.
I will undertake to make my remarks very brief.
There are several gentlemen absent who did not expect the agricultural estimates to come up.
This is about the most interesting subject that comes before us and we would like a full House to hear the Minister of Agriculture.
I have two or three small items in the customs.
Your items pass any time as a matter of course.

We can not make fish of one and flesh of another.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What are you going to do on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: After private Bills we hope to proceed with the Autonomy Bill.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11-05 p.m.
Monday, May 22, 1905.
